posts.author: rzeheb
posts.content_md: My lab (at work, not my holography setup which can be called a lot of things but not a lab) used to perform electron microscopy. Recently I ran across some EM film that was destined for the trash. I rescued it in the hopes that 300 sheets of 4 by 5 film might be useful for making holograms. The film "expired" in 2003 but that's not THAT old, probably just lost some sensitivity ![:pray:](https://holographyforum.org//cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/twitter/twemoji@latest/assets/svg/1f64f.svg) . It was stored in a refrigerator the whole time. The film is Kodak Estar Thickbase 4489 (emulsion No. 27200201). As far as I know, EM film is typically ultra fine grain and sensitive at the blue end of the spectrum. I am using a 532 nm laser. Anyone know what the spectral sensitivity of that film is, or else, can anyone suggest a resource where I might go to look it up?

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
I was hoping someone would awnser. I think you are going to have to shoot some trials. Set up two beams spread to fill the test piece at a 15 degree angle. Find the exposure time that causes the film to go dark in 60 seconds in the developer. Then try increasing the angle till you find out if you can have the beams at the oposite sides of the film. 

Also, take a bleached piece of film and see what the base does to the polarization of a laser. Once you have that data you can plan some shots.

posts.author: rzeheb
posts.content_md: Hi Colin. I, too, was hoping someone might have had some specific information on the spectral profile of that film. Prior to posting I had searched the web as thoroughly as I could. I also made numerous calls to Kodak, being transferred from person to person in the process and no one was able to answer what I thought was a pretty basic question. I guess it's not the Kodak it used to be. I had also tried a couple of test shots without success. At one point, in utter frustration, I actually passed the film through the unexpanded beam of a 5 mw green laser pointer and was barely able to darken the film in the areas where the beam passed!! However, I think the problem actually lies with my developer solution. I am using JD-2 from Integraf (it's the only developer I have). Kodak recommends D-19 for this film. I suppose that to move forward I will need to go out and get some D-19 (and fixative, and hypoclear) so that I can test this out with only one variable (the light). In any case, I very much appreciate your reply and suggestions, the implementation of which will have to wait until I get the chemicals. I'll report back on my results.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: I often use D-19, I don't fix or anything. I go from D-19 to traditional holographic bleaches with no problems.

posts.author: salvee
posts.content_md: From a quick web search, it seems as if the resolution of the film is 200 lines/mm. You need 2000 lines/mm for a transmission hologram and 5000 lines / mm for a reflection hologram. My advice is to stop wasting your time trying to make this film work for holography.

posts.author: Jeffrey Weil
posts.content_md:
Hello Everyone,

I have not looked up that film but the above info makes it pretty clear it won't work. BUT, its probably a nice film to convert to Jeff Blyth's diffusion method for home made film. 

If you look up the diffusion post or the wiki on this subject you'll see at the end it says as a short cut use already made film, just fix out the silver and reload the gelatin with the new chemistry. 

 Jeff Weil

 NorthBeach Holography Inc.
